01.note: A man owed a creditor one hundred dinars. He had two small tracts of land and sold both to one buyer, fifty dinars each. The creditor seized one tract toward the debt, then came back to seize the other. The buyer went to him with one hundred dinars and said: if the first tract is worth a hundred to you, keep it; if not, take the hundred dinars and give up your claim to both. Rav Yosef thought this matched a ruling in the mishna about orphans and the value of their father's property, but Abaye said the cases differ: here the creditor loses nothing, since he lent one hundred and gets back one hundred.
01.why: The Gemara has just told the same kind of case with two mansions and a thousand dinars. This smaller version repeats the comparison with the mishna, and the Gemara then asks what sum the buyer's claim against the seller is written for.

people.name: Rav Yosef
people.about: A Sage who first thought this case was the same as the one in the mishna.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: A Sage who argued the two cases are not alike, since the creditor loses nothing.

terms.meaning: A silver coin; sums of money in the story are counted in dinars.
The early collection of Jewish law that the Gemara discusses line by line. Here it refers to a ruling about orphans who offer to value their father's property higher than it is worth.

02.note: A man who owed a creditor one hundred dinars died, leaving only a small tract of land worth fifty dinars. The creditor seized it. His orphans paid the creditor fifty dinars and took the land back, and then the creditor seized it again for the rest of the debt. They came before Abaye, who told them that it is a mitzva for orphans to pay their father's debt: their first payment fulfilled that mitzva, and the creditor's second seizure was lawful.
02.why: This is one of a run of cases about creditors seizing sold or inherited land. Right after it the Gemara limits Abaye's ruling: had the orphans said the fifty dinars were payment for the land itself, the creditor would have had no further claim on it.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: The Sage the orphans came to; he ruled the creditor's second seizure was lawful.

terms.meaning: A religious duty or good deed commanded by Jewish law. Abaye says paying a dead father's debt is one for his children.

03.note: A man sold his right to collect his mother's marriage settlement in the future, telling the buyer that if his mother came and objected to the sale, he would not repay him. His mother died without objecting, and then he himself came to contest the sale. Rami bar Hama thought he stood in his mother's place and could object as she could. Rava answered him: he may not have guaranteed the sale against his mother's objection, but did he not guarantee it against his own?
03.why: The Gemara follows this with another ruling of Rami bar Hama about a sale guarantee, where Rava again objects, this time over whether a guarantee covers the buyer's own creditors.

people.name: Rami bar Ḥama
people.about: A Sage who first thought the son could object in his mother's place.

people.name: Rava
people.about: A Sage who answered that the son had guaranteed the sale against his own objections.

terms.meaning: The ketuba: a document promising a wife a sum from her husband's property if he dies or divorces her. Here the son sold his future right to collect his mother's.
A seller's promise to repay the buyer if the sale is later undone by someone else's claim.

04.note: Rami bar Hama's mother wrote a deed in the morning giving her property to Rami bar Hama, and in the evening wrote another giving it to her other son, Mar Ukva bar Hama. Rami went to Rav Sheshet, who awarded him the property; Mar Ukva went to Rav Nahman, who awarded it to him. Rav Sheshet asked Rav Nahman why. Rav Sheshet's reason was that Rami's deed came first; Rav Nahman replied that we do not live in Jerusalem, where the hour is written on documents. Rav Nahman's reason was the discretion of the judges. When Rav Sheshet claimed the same, Rav Nahman answered that he himself was a judge and Rav Sheshet was not, and that Rav Sheshet had not ruled on that basis to begin with.
04.why: The Gemara has been debating two deeds dated the same day, and a view that leaves such money to someone's discretion. This case shows two Sages split over the same-day deeds and the discretion of the judges.

people.name: Rami bar Ḥama
people.about: The son who received his mother's property by a deed written in the morning.

people.name: Mar Ukva bar Ḥama
people.about: His brother, who received the same property by a deed written that evening.

people.name: Rav Sheshet
people.about: The Sage who awarded the property to Rami bar Ḥama because his deed came first.

people.name: Rav Naḥman
people.about: The judge who awarded it to Mar Ukva, by the discretion of the judges.

terms.meaning: A written document transferring ownership of property; here two deeds give the same property to two sons.
A rule that when the law cannot decide between two claims, a judge may award the property to whoever he thinks the owner meant to have it.

05.note: Two deeds came before Rav Yosef for the same property: one dated the fifth of Nisan, the other just 'Nisan' with no day. Rav Yosef gave the property to the holder of the fifth-of-Nisan deed. The other man asked: should I lose? Rav Yosef said he was at a disadvantage, since his deed could be from the twenty-ninth. The man asked for a document letting him collect from the seller's later buyers, from Iyyar on. Rav Yosef replied that those buyers could say his deed was from the first of Nisan, so the field was rightly his. The Gemara gives his remedy: the two deed holders should write each other an authorization to collect.
05.why: The Gemara has just told of two deeds for the same property written on the same day, morning and evening; this is a second case of rival deeds, decided by how exactly each is dated.

people.name: Rav Yosef
people.about: The Sage before whom the two deeds came; he ruled for the holder of the dated deed.

terms.meaning: Months of the Hebrew calendar; Iyyar follows Nisan.
A court document that lets a creditor or buyer seize property, here from people who later bought land from the seller.

06.note: Someone left coral belonging to orphans in the care of a certain man. The man valued the coral for himself at four hundred dinars and took it. Its value then rose to six hundred dinars. He came before Rabbi Ammi, who asked him: who valued it for you?
06.why: The Gemara has just explained a ruling that a widow who valued property for herself accomplished nothing, because no one valued it for her; this incident is brought as a parallel, with the same question.

people.name: Rabbi Ammi
people.about: The Sage the man came to; he asked who had valued the coral for him.

terms.meaning: Property belonging to children whose father has died, which the court and those trusted with it must protect.

07.note: A man rented out his millstone to another, to be paid by the renter grinding for him. Later the owner became rich and bought another millstone and a donkey. He said to the renter: until now I had my grinding done by you; now give me money as rent. The renter answered: I will grind for you. The story itself does not say how the dispute ended.
07.why: Ravina compares the case to the mishna's rule that two men who must feed a girl cannot both feed her, so one pays money instead; Rav Avira rejects the comparison, since the owner can keep using the grinding.

terms.meaning: A heavy stone used to grind grain into flour.

08.note: As he was dying, Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi called his sons and told them to honor their (step)mother, to keep his lamp, table and bed in place, and that Yosef Heifani and Shimon Efrati, who served him in life, would serve him in death. He came home every Shabbat eve after his death, until a maidservant told a neighbor 'Rabbi is sitting,' and he came no more. He told the Sages where to eulogize him, to reopen the yeshiva after thirty days, that Gamliel would be Nasi and Hanina bar Hama head of the yeshiva. A launderer who missed his funeral threw himself from a roof and died, and was promised the World-to-Come. Rabbi Hiyya and Rabbi Hanina argued over who did more for Torah. Rabbi then passed on wisdom to Shimon and the Nasi's office to Gamliel.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: The dying leader who gives his sons and the Sages his last instructions.

people.name: Rabbi Shimon
people.about: His younger son, called a Sage; Rabbi passes the orders of wisdom to him.

people.name: Rabban Gamliel
people.about: His older son, whom he appoints Nasi.

people.name: Rabbi Ḥanina
people.about: Named by Rabbi to head the yeshiva; he argues with Rabbi Ḥiyya.

people.name: Rabbi Ḥiyya
people.about: A Sage praised by Rabbi for teaching Torah to children in towns without teachers.

terms.meaning: The head of the Jewish community in the Land of Israel, an office Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi held and passed to his son.
A voice from Heaven that announces a decision or message.
The life after death promised to the righteous.
A house of Torah study.

08.flag: Very long span: interleaves the deathbed narrative with long stretches of Gemara analysis, and contains the launderer and Rabbi Ḥanina episodes that are also coded separately (7B7829, 3DE90C).

09.note: On the day of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's funeral, a Divine Voice announced that everyone present at it was destined for life in the World-to-Come. A launderer who came to Rabbi every day had not come that day. When he heard this, he went up to a roof, fell to the ground and died. A Divine Voice announced: that launderer too is destined for life in the World-to-Come.
09.why: It comes in the Gemara's account of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's death, right after its explanation of his instructions on how he was to be eulogized and mourned.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: The great Sage, called simply Rabbi, whose funeral this is.

people.name: the launderer
people.about: A man who came before Rabbi every day but missed his funeral.

terms.meaning: A voice from Heaven that announces a decision or message.
The life after death promised to the righteous.

10.note: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi had instructed that Hanina bar Hama sit at the head of the yeshiva. Rabbi Hanina refused, because Rabbi Afes was two and a half years older than him. So Rabbi Afes sat at the head, Rabbi Hanina sat outside, and Levi came and sat with him. When Rabbi Afes died, Rabbi Hanina took the head seat, Levi had no one to sit with, and he came to Babylonia. Rav was told that a great man who limps had come to Neharde'a and taught that a woman may go out on Shabbat wearing a kelila. Rav concluded that Rabbi Afes had died, Rabbi Hanina had taken his place, and Levi had come.
10.why: The Gemara is explaining Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's dying instructions one by one; this is how his instruction about Hanina bar Hama came true. The Gemara then asks how Rav knew it was Rabbi Afes, not Rabbi Hanina, who had died.

people.name: Rabbi Ḥanina
people.about: Ḥanina bar Ḥama, named by Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi to head the yeshiva; he deferred to the older Rabbi Afes.

people.name: Rabbi Afes
people.about: An older Sage who sat at the head of the yeshiva until he died.

people.name: Levi
people.about: A Sage who limps; he studied with Rabbi Ḥanina, then came to Babylonia.

people.name: Rav
people.about: A Sage in Babylonia who worked out from the news what had happened.

terms.meaning: A house of Torah study; sitting at its head means leading it.
A tiara-like ornament; Levi taught that a woman may wear it in the public domain on Shabbat.

11.note: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi lay ill in Tzippori. On the day he died the Sages fasted and prayed for him, and said anyone who announced his death would be stabbed with a sword. His maidservant first prayed that the lower world would win; seeing his suffering, she prayed the upper world would win. When the Sages would not stop praying, she threw a jug from the roof; in the moment of silence, Rabbi died. Bar Kappara, sent to check, found him dead, tore his clothes and hid the tear, and told the Sages that the angels had seized the holy ark. 'He died?' they asked. 'You said it, I did not.' Dying, Rabbi raised ten fingers and said he had toiled in Torah and taken no benefit. A Divine Voice answered: 'He enters in peace.'
11.why: This closes the Gemara's long account of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's death. The verse the Divine Voice quotes then leads into teachings about how angels go out to greet the righteous and the wicked when they die.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: The great Sage, called Rabbi, whose death this is.

people.name: the maidservant of Rabbi
people.about: His servant, who prays for his release and silences the Sages' prayers.

people.name: bar Kappara
people.about: A Sage sent to check on Rabbi, who breaks the news without saying it.

terms.meaning: Tefillin: small leather boxes holding verses, worn during prayer and study; Rabbi removed them each time he went to the bathroom.
A voice from Heaven that announces a decision or message.
A sign of mourning made on hearing of a death.

12.note: Rav Hiyya Arikha's mother-in-law was also his brother's widow. For twenty-five years he supported her in her father's house from his brother's estate. Then she asked for support, and he refused; she asked for her marriage payment, and he said she had lost that too. Rabba bar Sheila ruled that she had not asked out of embarrassment, and ordered him to pay. When he refused, Rabba bar Sheila authorized her to seize his property. Rav Hiyya went to Rava, who said the ruling was good. She then asked Rava for the produce of the land since then. Rava found the authorization did not say the land came from the dead husband's estate, ruled it badly written, and denied her any produce, rejecting her plea to treat the omission as a scribal error.
12.why: The Gemara has been discussing when a widow loses the right to her marriage payment by long delay. This case applies that to a widow supported for twenty-five years in her father's house, and ends with how an authorization to seize property must be written.

people.name: Rav Ḥiyya Arikha
people.about: A Sage who supported his brother's widow, also his mother-in-law, for twenty-five years.

people.name: Rabba bar Sheila
people.about: The judge who ordered him to pay her marriage payment and wrote the authorization.

people.name: Rava
people.about: A Sage who upheld the ruling but found the authorization badly written.

terms.meaning: The ketuba: a document promising a wife a sum from her husband's property if he dies or divorces her.
A court document letting a creditor seize a debtor's property in payment.
A mistake by the writer of a document, which a court may treat as if the missing words were written.

13.note: Rabbi Yishmael son of Rabbi Yosei had a sharecropper who brought him a basket of fruit every Shabbat eve. One week he brought it on Thursday, explaining that he had a case to bring before him and was coming anyway. Rabbi Yishmael refused the fruit and said he was disqualified from judging the case. He seated two other scholars to judge it, but as he came and went he kept thinking of arguments the sharecropper could make. He said: blast the souls of those who take bribes. If I, who took nothing, and would only have taken what was mine, feel this way, how much more those who take bribes.
13.why: The Gemara has taught that even a small favor counts as a bribe, with judges who stepped aside after someone helped them. This case shows that even a gift that is refused leaves the judge biased.

people.name: Rabbi Yishmael son of Rabbi Yosei
people.about: A Sage and judge who refused his sharecropper's early gift of fruit.

people.name: the sharecropper
people.about: A man who farmed Rabbi Yishmael's land and brought him fruit each week.

terms.meaning: A farmer who works someone else's land and pays the owner with part of the crop.
Friday, the day before the Sabbath.

14.note: A man brought Rabbi Yishmael bar Elisha, a priest, the first shearing of his sheep. Rabbi Yishmael asked where he was from, and why he had not given it to a priest closer to home. The man said he had a case to bring before him and had brought the gift on the way. Rabbi Yishmael said he was disqualified from judging the case and would not accept the gift. He seated two other scholars to judge it, but as he came and went he kept thinking of arguments the man could make. He said: blast the souls of those who take bribes. If I, who took nothing, and would only have taken what I was owed as a priest, feel this way, how much more those who take bribes.
14.why: It follows an almost identical case about Rabbi Yishmael son of Rabbi Yosei and his sharecropper's fruit, in a series of judges who stepped aside after receiving even a small gift or favor.

people.name: Rabbi Yishmael bar Elisha
people.about: A priest and judge who refused a gift from a man with a case before him.

terms.meaning: The first wool shorn from a flock each year, which the Torah says to give to a priest.
A kohen, a descendant of Aaron, entitled to certain gifts from other Jews.

15.note: A man brought Rav Anan a basket of small fish and said he had a case to bring. Rav Anan refused and said he was disqualified. The man said he did not need his judgment; he only wanted to give a gift, since a gift to a Torah scholar is like bringing first fruits. Rav Anan accepted it and sent him to Rav Nahman with a note saying he could not judge this man. Rav Nahman concluded the man was Rav Anan's relative, set aside a case of orphans to hear his, and the other side, seeing the honor shown, could not argue and lost. Elijah the prophet, who had been teaching Rav Anan, stopped coming. Rav Anan fasted and prayed and Elijah came back, but frightened him, so Rav Anan made a box and sat in it while Elijah taught him the rest.
15.why: It ends the Gemara's series of judges who refused cases after receiving a gift or favor; here the gift was taken for a good reason, yet it still led another judge to pervert a case.

people.name: Rav Anan
people.about: A Sage who accepted a man's gift and sent his case to another judge.

people.name: Rav Naḥman
people.about: The judge who took the man for Rav Anan's relative and heard his case first.

people.name: Elijah
people.about: The prophet, who used to visit Rav Anan to teach him.

terms.meaning: The first ripe produce of the year, which the Torah says to bring to the Temple.
A commandment to do something; Rav Naḥman weighed judging fairly against honoring Torah scholars.
A book of teachings said to come from Elijah, in a longer and a shorter part.

16.note: In Rav Yosef's years there was a time of divine anger, a famine. The Sages asked him to pray for mercy. He answered: if the prophet Elisha, who supported 2,200 Sages out of his own pocket, did not pray for mercy in a time of anger, should I?
16.why: Rav Yosef's figure of 2,200 Sages comes from the verse about Elisha's servant setting loaves before a hundred men; the Gemara goes on to derive the number from it and to list how many students stayed on at later academies.

people.name: Rav Yosef
people.about: A Sage asked to pray during a famine, who refused.

people.name: Elisha
people.about: The prophet, who Rav Yosef says supported 2,200 Sages and did not pray in a time of anger.

terms.meaning: Asking God to cancel a harsh decree, such as a famine.

17.note: A man had used a field as a boundary marker in a deed, describing it as someone else's. Later he claimed the field as his own, and then he died, leaving a steward over his orphans' property. The steward came before Abaye, who said the man had lost his claim. The steward said that the father would have claimed he meant only one furrow; Abaye agreed, citing Rabbi Yohanan, and told him to hand over one furrow. That furrow held a row of palm trees, so the steward said the father would have claimed he sold the field and bought it back; Abaye agreed again. Abaye then said: whoever appoints a steward should appoint one like this, who knows how to argue for orphans.
17.why: The mishna taught that one who names a field as a marker for another loses his claim to it, and Abaye has just limited that rule. This case shows the rule applied, and the claims Rabbi Yohanan allows against it.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: The Sage who judged the case and praised the steward.

people.name: the steward
people.about: The man appointed to look after the dead man's orphans' property.

people.name: Rabbi Yoḥanan
people.about: A Sage whose rulings Abaye cites to accept the steward's claims.

terms.meaning: A neighboring field named in a deed to show where another field's boundary lies; naming it as someone else's admits it is theirs.
A person appointed to manage the property of orphans.

18.note: Rav Yosef told of a man in Shihin whose father left him three branches of mustard. One broke, and on it alone they found nine kav of mustard, and with its wood they roofed a booth for craftsmen. Rabbi Shimon ben Tahlifa said his father left them a cabbage stalk so tall they went up and down it with a ladder.
18.why: The Gemara is describing how fruitful the Land of Israel will be in the future, and tells these incidents, like the fox in the giant turnip before them, so the reader will not be surprised.

people.name: Rav Yosef
people.about: The Sage who tells of the giant mustard plant.

people.name: Rabbi Shimon ben Taḥlifa
people.about: A Sage who tells of a cabbage stalk his father left.

terms.meaning: A measure of dry volume, roughly a liter or two.
A teaching of the early Sages not included in the Mishna, quoted by the Gemara.

19.note: Rav Hiyya bar Adda taught Reish Lakish's children. Once he stayed away for three days. When he came, Reish Lakish asked why. He said his father had left him one grapevine branch: the first day he picked three hundred clusters, each giving a jugful of wine; the second day three hundred more, two to a jug; the third day three hundred, three to a jug, and he declared more than half ownerless. Reish Lakish told him that had he not stayed away, the vine would have yielded more.
19.why: The Gemara is collecting stories about the great bounty of the Land of Israel, after expounding verses about its wine.

people.name: Rav Ḥiyya bar Adda
people.about: A teacher of children for Reish Lakish, who stayed away three days to harvest a vine.

people.name: Reish Lakish
people.about: A Sage who employed him and asked why he had been away.

terms.meaning: Gave up ownership so that anyone, especially the poor, may take it.

20.note: Rami bar Yehezkel came to Benei Berak and saw goats grazing under a fig tree. Honey was oozing from the figs and milk was dripping from the goats, and the two were mixing. He said: this is what the verse means by 'a land flowing with milk and honey.'
20.why: It is one of a series of reports of the bounty of the Land of Israel; other Sages follow with their own sightings of land flowing with milk and honey.

people.name: Rami bar Yeḥezkel
people.about: A Sage who visited Benei Berak and saw the verse come true.
